amdahl1967.title: Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities
amdahl1967.author: Gene M. Amdahl
amdahl1967.venue: AFIPS Conference Proceedings, Vol. 30, Spring Joint Computer Conference, Atlantic City, N.J., Apr. 18-20, 1967, pp. 483-485 (DOI 10.1145/1465482.1465560)
amdahl1967.quote: Reprinted from the AFIPS Conference Proceedings, Vol. 30 (Atlantic City, N.J., Apr. 18-20), AFIPS Press, Reston, Va., 1967, pp. 483-485, when Dr. Amdahl was at International Business Machines Corporation, Sunnyvale, California. // "Demonstration is made of the continued validity of the single processor approach and of the weaknesses of the multiple processor approach in terms of application to real problems and their attendant irregularities." // "The first characteristic of interest is the fraction of the computational load which is associated with data management housekeeping. This fraction has been very nearly constant for about ten years, and accounts for 40% of the executed instructions in production runs." // "The nature of this overhead appears to be sequential so that it is unlikely to be amenable to parallel processing techniques. Overhead alone would then place an upper limit on throughput of five to seven times the sequential processing rate, even if the housekeeping were done in a separate processor." // "A fairly obvious conclusion which can be drawn at this point is that the effort expended on achieving high parallel processing rates is wasted unless it is accompanied by achievements in sequential processing rates of very nearly the same magnitude." // "Machine A has thirty two arithmetic execution units controlled by a single instruction stream." // "The performance of these three machines is plotted in Figure I as a function of the fraction of the number of instructions which permit parallelism. The probable region of operation is centered around a point corresponding to 25% data management overhead and 10% of the problem operations forced to be sequential." // "If alternatively one decided to improve the performance by putting two processors side by side with shared memory, one would find approximately 2.2 times as much hardware. The additional two tenths in hardware accomplish the crossbar switching for the sharing. The resulting performance achieved would be about 1.8. The latter figure is derived from the assumption of each processor utilizing half of the memories about half of the time. The resulting memory conflicts in the shared system would extend the execution of one of two operations by one quarter of the execution time. The net result is a price performance degradation to 0.8 rather than an improvement to 2.0 for the single larger processor." // Editors' note on the same reprint: "This article was the first publication by Gene Amdahl on what became known as Amdahl's Law. Interestingly, it has no equations and only a single figure."
amdahl1967.note: Read as the full-text reprint in IEEE SSCS News, Summer 2007, pp. 19-20, which reproduces the 1967 AFIPS paper verbatim and prints the original bibliographic header. Re-opened and re-transcribed independently on 2026-08-22 (verification pass). The OCR of the scan renders '10%' as 'l0%'; the printed figure is a lowercase L for the digit one. The 'no equations and only a single figure' characterisation is the 2007 SSCS editors', not Amdahl's, and is corroborated by reading the reprinted body text. IMPORTANT ordering note: the five-to-seven-times bound is derived in the paper from the 40%-of-executed-instructions housekeeping figure (reducible by a factor of two, 'highly improbably' by three), stated two paragraphs BEFORE the '25% data management overhead and 10% of the problem operations forced to be sequential' sentence, which locates the probable region of operation on Figure I for three specific machine organizations. Neither 25% nor 10% yields five to seven, and the paper does not chain them; the prose therefore uses only the 40% figure. The Rattner caption printed under the redrawn figure in the 2007 reprint restates the two percentages the other way round ('25% of the computation to be sequential ... overhead ... averaging 10%'); that caption is a 2007 gloss and is not used.
supports: pages 483-485, AFIPS Conference Proceedings vol. 30, Atlantic City, N.J., 18-20 April 1967
Amdahl was at International Business Machines Corporation, Sunnyvale, California
three printed pages, one figure, no equations
the paper promises a demonstration of 'the weaknesses of the multiple processor approach'
data management housekeeping accounts for 40% of the executed instructions in production runs
upper limit on throughput of five to seven times the sequential processing rate, even if the housekeeping were done in a separate processor

bouknight1972.title: The Illiac IV System
bouknight1972.author: W. J. Bouknight, Stewart A. Denenberg, David E. McIntyre, J. M. Randall, Amed H. Sameh, Daniel L. Slotnick
bouknight1972.venue: Proceedings of the IEEE, Vol. 60, No. 4, April 1972, pp. 369-388 (invited paper)
bouknight1972.quote: "The Illiac IV project was started in the Computer Science Department at the University of Illinois with the objective of developing a digital system employing the principle of parallel operation to achieve a computational rate of 10^9 instructions/s. In order to achieve this rate, the system was to employ 256 processors operating simultaneously under a central control divided into four subassembly quadrants of 64 processors each. Due primarily to subcontractor problems several basic technological changes were necessitated during the course of the program, principally, reduction in individual logic-circuit complexity and memory technology. These resulted in cost escalation and schedule delays, ultimately limiting the system to one quadrant with an overall speed of approximately 200 million instructions/s. It is this one-quadrant system that will be discussed for the remainder of this paper." // "As stated in the Introduction, the original design of Illiac IV contained four CUs, each of which controlled a 64-ALU array processor. The version being built by the Burroughs Corporation will have only one CU which drives 64 ALUs as shown in Fig. 3." // "Each PE performs the same operation under command from the CU in the lock-stepped manner of an array processor. That is, since there is only one CU, there is only one instruction stream and all of the ALUs respond together or are lock-stepped to the current instruction. If the current instruction is ADD for example, then all the ALUs will add - there can be no instruction which will cause some of the ALUs to be adding while others are multiplying." // "Since this register is under the programmer's control, individual PEs within the array of 64 PEs may be set to enabled (active) or disabled (passive) status based on the contents of one of the other PE registers. For example, there are instructions which disable all PEs whose RGR contents are greater than their RGA contents. Only those PEs in an enabled state are able to execute the current instruction." // "The Illiac IV system is scheduled for completion by the end of this calendar year; the fabrication phase is essentially complete with some final assembly and considerable debugging yet to be completed." // "All of this work was sponsored under a Grant (Contract USAF 30(602)4144) from the Advanced Research Projects Agency." // "The logical design of Illiac IV is patterned after that of the Solomon [2], [3] computers, prototypes of which were built by the Westinghouse Electric Corporation in the early 1960's." // Reference list, item [3]: "D. L. Slotnick, 'Unconventional systems,' in 1967 Spring Joint Computer Conf. AFIPS Conf. Proc. Washington, D. C.: Spartan, 1967, pp. 477-481." // "These formidable design, programming, and operating efforts were under the direction of Arthur B. Carroll, who, during this period, was the project's deputy principal investigator."
bouknight1972.note: Read as the scanned IEEE Xplore PDF mirrored by the University of Auckland; re-downloaded and re-read independently on 2026-08-22 (verification pass). Running head confirms 'PROCEEDINGS OF THE IEEE, VOL. 60, NO. 4, APRIL 1972', pp. 369-388, 'Invited Paper'. The scan's OCR mangles spacing and renders 'PEs' as 'PES' and the exponent in 10^9 as 'IO9'; quotes above are transcribed with those OCR artefacts corrected and nothing else changed. Daniel L. Slotnick is a co-author, so the 'cost escalation and schedule delays' wording is the project's own. The paper names Arthur B. Carroll as deputy principal investigator and names no principal investigator, so it does not establish who led the project. It cites Slotnick's 'Unconventional systems' (1967, pp. 477-481) as a SOLOMON-lineage reference, NOT among the references it gives for the Illiac IV architecture ([4]-[6]) - which is why no claim about the content of that talk appears in the chapter.

dblp_afips67.note: Used only for the position of Slotnick's talk in the same volume: pp. 477-481, DOI 10.1145/1465482.1465559, immediately preceding Amdahl's pp. 483-485, DOI 10.1145/1465482.1465560. The paper itself was not opened - ACM DL returns 403 - so nothing is quoted from its contents. On re-check (2026-08-22) dblp itself returned 503, so the page range was re-verified against two independent records: Crossref's DOI metadata for both DOIs (start pages 477 and 483, consecutive DOIs, event 'the April 18-20, 1967, spring joint computer conference'), and the reference list of Bouknight et al. 1972, which prints 'pp. 477-481' for the same talk. Both are quoted above / in the bouknight1972 entry.
supports: Slotnick's "Unconventional systems" occupies pp. 477-481 of AFIPS vol. 30, immediately before Amdahl's pp. 483-485

unverified: The content of Daniel Slotnick's talk "Unconventional systems" (AFIPS 1967, pp. 477-481). ACM DL returns 403 and no other copy was found, so the talk was not opened. An earlier draft of this story attributed the 256-processor/four-quadrant/10^9-instructions-per-second plan to that talk on the strength of Bouknight et al. 1972; that is a five-year-later source, and Bouknight et al. in fact cite the talk as a SOLOMON-lineage reference rather than among their references for the Illiac IV architecture. No claim about what the talk said now appears in the prose or on any card - only its printed position in the volume.

That Daniel Slotnick led, or was principal investigator of, the ILLIAC IV project. Bouknight et al. 1972 name Arthur B. Carroll as the project's 'deputy principal investigator' and name no principal investigator; Slotnick's 1982 IEEE Annals memoir (pp. 20-30) is paywalled and was not opened. What is verified is that Slotnick co-authored the project's own 1972 Proc. IEEE paper and the 1962 SOLOMON paper whose design ILLIAC IV is patterned after. The chapter claims only that.

That Amdahl's five-to-seven-times bound follows from his '25% data management overhead and 10% of the problem operations forced to be sequential' probable case. It does not: the bound is derived from the separate 40%-housekeeping figure. The 25%/10% pair belongs to Figure I and is not used in the prose.

That ILLIAC IV was finished or delivered. The April 1972 paper is written in the future tense about completion - the one-CU version is 'being built by the Burroughs Corporation' and the system is 'scheduled for completion by the end of this calendar year' with 'considerable debugging yet to be completed'. Nothing accessible confirms the completion date, so the prose says the machine 'went ahead', not that it shipped or ran.

The widely repeated budget figures - $8 million estimated in 1966 rising to $31 million - trace to Daniel Slotnick's 1982 IEEE Annals of the History of Computing memoir, p. 27, via secondary summaries. The memoir is paywalled and was not opened; secondary summaries disagree on whether the $31 million total is dated to 1971 or 1972. No dollar figure appears in the prose.

That Amdahl's 1967 paper was written specifically as a rebuttal to ILLIAC IV, or that he spoke immediately after Slotnick at the podium. The paper names neither ILLIAC IV nor Slotnick. What is verified is printed order in the volume: Slotnick pp. 477-481, Amdahl pp. 483-485, consecutive DOIs. The prose claims only the printed order.
The April 1972 delivery of ILLIAC IV to NASA Ames and its installation in building N-233 (attributed to Hord 1982, p. 7). Hord's book was not obtainable. NASA Ames is not named in the prose.
That ILLIAC IV first ran reliably or in production in 1975, and that it was switched off on 7 September 1981.
That student protest at the University of Illinois over classified DoD work caused the machine to be moved off campus.
The often-quoted claim that ILLIAC IV's delivered performance was 15 MFLOPS against a 1000 MFLOPS prediction. Only the instruction-rate figures in Bouknight et al. 1972 were confirmed.
Gene Amdahl's job title at IBM Sunnyvale in April 1967. The reprint header gives the employer and city only.
